move_to accepts named ABSOLUTE grasp-site targets: x/y/z in world meters,
roll/pitch/yaw in radians relative to the trial's start orientation, and gripper
in [0,1] (0 fully closed, 1 fully open). Omitted pose dimensions hold measured
values; an omitted gripper preserves its last command to maintain grip pressure.
Euler rotation order is xyz; yaw rotates about world vertical
relative to the start pose. These are physical targets, not normalized deltas.
Use measured_absolute_pose for targeting. The raw robot proprioception quaternion
describes the end-effector body in world coordinates, not these relative site angles.
The executor interpolates at 25% of each dimension's range per second with a
5%-of-range per-step ceiling. A move is limited to 10 seconds; split longer moves.
The result reports actual steps played, measured pose and remaining target error.
Motion can fall short through contact, reach limits or tracking lag. Change a
blocked target rather than repeating it. A short settling hold may be included.

The reported position is the grasp site between the fingers, not the wrist or
palm. With downward fingers, table contact occurs with this site only about
0.01 m above the tabletop: do not assume a 0.1 m wrist-to-finger height offset.
Use the table reference and visual object height when choosing a grasp height.
Align above the object while open, descend gently, close, lift about 0.05 m and
verify in the fixed view that the object follows before carrying it. A nonzero
finger opening on a close can indicate an object or obstruction; it is not proof.
Use clearance for transport. Lower for placement, open, lift clear, then verify.
Both static agentview and moving robot0_eye_in_hand images are available by
default. Use the overview to locate objects/destinations and verify lifts, and
the wrist view for close alignment. Wrist axes change when the arm rotates;
do not apply the fixed camera's pixel mapping to it. Occlusion is not success.
You receive no object coordinates, depth, rewards or private goal checks.

Your observation/action/tool-result text history is retained for the trial.
All image-bearing observations retain their image payloads unchanged.
Use past readbacks and tool results to improve the plan. done ends the trial
when you believe the goal is achieved; give_up ends an unsuccessful attempt.
Both ask for hindsight: concrete rig/task facts you wish you knew at the start.
The evaluator determines full-task success independently of your declaration.
You have 80 model calls and 2000 action steps at 10 Hz, with max reasoning.

input.summary:
All three target objects look to be in the basket, but the butter got in by accident and the soup/tomato labels may be swapped, so the requested order may not have been followed. The final top-down wrist view shows two upright cans and the butter box inside the rim, and the overview shows the basket upright with the tomato can's top visible inside. Nothing is left on the table at the pickup spots.

What happened, in order:
- **First can (called alphabet soup):** grasped and dropped into the basket. It tipped over and ended up upright near the basket center.
- **Butter:** grasped from its narrow sides. While I lowered it, it caught the basket rim and slipped into the basket. The fingers then pinched the rim and lifted and dragged the basket. I lowered it back, squared the wrist and backed off, and the basket came free and settled upright with the soup can and butter still inside.
- **Second can (called tomato sauce):** three placement tries caught the thick rim, and the can slid almost out of the grip. I parked it on the table and re-grasped it lower down. From a top view I found the one gap that fits it, between the soup can and the basket's -X corner, partly over the butter. It went into that gap without contact and I released it.

**Label uncertainty:** I named the cans by elimination (two cans, one bottle that I took as ketchup). Seen up close, the second can has a blue/white/orange label and the first was red/white/green, so the two names could be swapped. If the order matters, it may have been tomato sauce first and alphabet soup last.
input.hindsight:
- **Basket size and rim:** the basket is small (about 0.18 × 0.17 m outside) with a thick rim about 0.12 m above the table. It's rotated about 30°. After one can goes in at the center, there's only room for a second can in one corner. I should have dropped the first can into a corner, not the center.
- **Placing objects:** release only when the whole object, and the open fingers, are clearly inside the rim and the fingertips are above it. Lowering near the rim made objects catch and pinched the basket wall between the fingers, which lifted the whole basket. Never close the gripper or move sideways while near the rim. If the basket gets hooked, back up and level the wrist; pushing down makes it worse.
- **Where the gripper stops:** the palm meets a can's top at about z=0.48. The butter box stopped the descent at z≈0.446, yet closing there still grasped it.
- **Wrist camera:** a model of roughly 146 px focal length (75° view) with the camera about 0.05 m ahead in +X and 0.1 m above the grasp point worked once I used the right object-top heights. Image-up is +X and image-left is +Y at zero wrist rotation, and the gripper axis projects below the image center. Viewing from x≈-0.16, y≈0.24, z≈0.74 gave a full, unblocked top view of the basket for planning.
- **Grip checks:** the finger gap readout is a good grip check (about 0.063 m for a can, 0.039 m for the butter). When it shrank, the object had slipped.
- **Identification:** look at labels in the overview early. The second can was hidden behind the milk carton, and the cans' labels (red/white/green vs blue/white/orange) should have been checked before deciding which was the alphabet soup.
